name: Cusco
tagline: Inca stone, colonial bells and the gateway to Machu Picchu
description:
Once the capital of the Inca Empire, Cusco sits in a bowl of green mountains at 3,400 meters, its streets still lined with the Incas' astonishingly precise stone walls. The Spanish built churches and mansions directly on top, so a single block can reveal polished Inca masonry, carved wooden balconies and a baroque bell tower all at once.

Most travelers come for Machu Picchu, reached by train through the Urubamba gorge, but Cusco itself deserves several unhurried days. Wander the steep lanes of San Blas with its artisans' workshops, climb to the colossal zigzag walls of Sacsayhuamán and head into the Sacred Valley for Sunday markets, shimmering salt pans and terraced ruins. Adventurers can tackle the multi-day Inca Trail or a dawn trek to the striped slopes of Rainbow Mountain.

Andean culture is vibrantly alive here. Women in embroidered hats sell hand-woven textiles, Quechua is spoken alongside Spanish, and festivals like Inti Raymi fill the plazas with dancers in dazzling costume. The food scene punches far above its size, from roast guinea pig and market soups to inventive tasting menus built on native potatoes, quinoa and alpaca. Take the altitude slowly, sip coca tea and let the thin air and vast skies work their magic.

safety.notes: Cusco is generally safe, but pickpockets work the markets and crowded plazas, and bag snatching happens late at night. Use registered taxis or ride apps after dark, and treat altitude sickness as the biggest real risk.

tipping: Tip around 10% in sit-down restaurants when service isn't included, and budget for tipping trekking guides, cooks and porters, which is customary and an important part of their income.
gettingAround: The historic center is compact and best explored on foot, though the 3,400-meter altitude makes every staircase count. Taxis are cheap if you agree on the fare first or use an app, and trains to Machu Picchu leave from Poroy near Cusco or from Ollantaytambo in the Sacred Valley.
tips: Consider spending your first night or two in the lower Sacred Valley (around 2,900 meters) and working up to Cusco, drinking plenty of water and coca tea along the way.
Machu Picchu tickets are timed and split into circuits, and Inca Trail permits sell out months ahead; book both as soon as your dates are fixed, and note the trail closes every February.
The Boleto Turístico covers Sacsayhuamán, Pisac, Moray, Ollantaytambo and more, but not Qorikancha or the cathedral, which have their own tickets.
Pack layers: dry-season days are sunny and warm, but nights can drop below freezing, and many older buildings have little heating.
Women and children posing with baby llamas expect a tip of a sol or two for photos, so agree before you snap.
Don't drink the tap water; most hotels offer filtered refills, which saves money and plastic.
etiquette: Always ask before photographing people, especially women in traditional dress, and expect to offer a small tip.
Bargain gently at markets; a few soles matter far more to the seller than to you.
Don't climb on Inca walls or stray from marked paths at archaeological sites, where guards strictly enforce the rules.
If someone pours a few drops of chicha on the ground before drinking, they're offering it to Pachamama, Mother Earth; feel free to do the same.

neighborhoods.name: Centro Histórico
neighborhoods.blurb: The UNESCO-listed core around the Plaza de Armas, where Inca walls form the foundations of colonial churches, mansions and balconied restaurants.

neighborhoods.name: San Blas
neighborhoods.blurb: The steep artisans' quarter above the plaza, all whitewashed houses, blue doors, craft workshops, cafés and cozy bars.

neighborhoods.name: San Cristóbal
neighborhoods.blurb: A hillside barrio just below Sacsayhuamán whose church terrace gives one of the finest panoramas over the city's terracotta roofs.

neighborhoods.name: San Pedro
neighborhoods.blurb: The bustling market district near the old train station, home to the city's main food market and cheap, hearty local eateries.

neighborhoods.name: Santa Ana
neighborhoods.blurb: A traditional residential neighborhood on the northwest slope, with a colonial church, stepped streets and very few tourists.

dishes.name: Cuy al horno
dishes.description: Whole guinea pig roasted until the skin crackles, a festive Andean dish often served with stuffed rocoto peppers and potatoes.

dishes.name: Adobo cusqueño
dishes.description: Pork marinated in chicha de jora, garlic and spices, then slow-simmered and eaten as a hearty Sunday breakfast with bread.

dishes.name: Chicharrón cusqueño
dishes.description: Chunks of pork simmered in their own fat until crisp, piled with giant-kernel corn, fried potatoes and fresh mint.

dishes.name: Chiriuchu
dishes.description: A cold festival platter for Corpus Christi of guinea pig, chicken, sausage, seaweed, cheese, roe and corn cakes; the name means 'cold chili' in Quechua.

dishes.name: Chicha de jora
dishes.description: A mildly alcoholic fermented corn beer brewed since Inca times, sold in homes that hang a red flag or flowers on a pole outside.

events.name: Corpus Christi
events.description: Fifteen saints and virgins from surrounding parishes are paraded into the Plaza de Armas and the cathedral, followed by a feast of chiriuchu.

events.name: Inti Raymi
events.description: On June 24, a grand reenactment of the Inca Festival of the Sun moves from Qorikancha to the Plaza de Armas and culminates at Sacsayhuamán.

events.name: Virgen del Carmen in Paucartambo
events.description: For several days in mid-July, masked dance troupes fill the streets of this mountain town a few hours from Cusco in one of Peru's wildest fiestas.

events.name: Santurantikuy
events.description: On December 24, the Plaza de Armas becomes a vast Christmas market of handmade nativity figures, ceramics and holiday treats.

attractions.name: Machu Picchu
attractions.description: The Incas' cloud-wrapped citadel clings to a saddle between jagged green peaks high above the Urubamba River, its temples and terraces fitted together without mortar. Catch an early bus to watch the mist lift off the ruins, or earn the view by hiking the Inca Trail to the Sun Gate.
attractions.bookingTip: Timed, circuit-based tickets sell out weeks ahead in high season, so book entry, train and the shuttle bus from Aguas Calientes together.

attractions.name: Sacsayhuamán
attractions.description: Colossal limestone blocks, some weighing well over 100 tons, lock together in three zigzag terraces on the hill above Cusco, an engineering feat still debated today. The grassy esplanade offers sweeping views over the city's rooftops and hosts the Inti Raymi ceremony every June.
attractions.bookingTip: Buy the partial tourist ticket covering Sacsayhuamán and three nearby ruins, and walk up slowly from San Cristóbal church to acclimatize.

attractions.name: Qorikancha
attractions.description: The Incas' holiest temple once had walls sheathed in gold; the conquistadors stripped it and built the Santo Domingo convent on top. Later earthquakes toppled much of the colonial building yet left the flawlessly fitted Inca chambers standing, the city's clearest lesson in who built better.
attractions.bookingTip: Hire one of the licensed guides at the entrance to decode the stonework, then stroll the sunken garden below.

attractions.name: Plaza de Armas
attractions.description: The Inca ceremonial square of Huacaypata is now Cusco's grand colonial plaza, framed by stone arcades, carved wooden balconies and the twin baroque facades of the cathedral and the Jesuit church. Return after dark, when the churches glow gold against the black hills.
attractions.bookingTip: For the best photos, grab a balcony table at one of the upstairs cafés overlooking the square at dusk.

attractions.name: Cusco Cathedral
attractions.description: Built partly with stones hauled from Sacsayhuamán, the cathedral holds hundreds of Cusco School paintings, including a Last Supper where Christ and the apostles dine on roast guinea pig. Silver altars and carved cedar choir stalls add to the overwhelming grandeur.
attractions.bookingTip: Buy the religious circuit ticket, which also covers San Blas church and the Archbishop's Palace, and rent the audio guide.

attractions.name: Twelve-Angled Stone
attractions.description: Set into the wall of an Inca palace on Hatun Rumiyoc street, this green diorite block meets its neighbors along twelve perfect angles without a hair's gap. It's a small sight, but one that makes Inca masonry suddenly tangible.
attractions.bookingTip: Tip a sol or two if you photograph the man in Inca costume who often stands beside it, then continue uphill into San Blas.

attractions.name: Museo de Arte Precolombino
attractions.description: Housed in a colonial mansion on a quiet plaza, this beautifully lit museum presents pre-Columbian gold, ceramics and textiles as fine art rather than dusty artifacts. Moche portrait vessels and shimmering featherwork are the highlights.
attractions.bookingTip: It stays open late, so save it for an evening or for when the afternoon rain rolls in.

attractions.name: Rainbow Mountain
attractions.description: Mineral-streaked slopes of red, ochre, turquoise and lavender rise above 5,000 meters in the Vilcanota range, a three-hour drive and a steep, breathless hike from Cusco. The glacier-capped bulk of Ausangate behind the stripes rewards every step.
attractions.bookingTip: Acclimatize for at least three days in Cusco first, take a 4 a.m. departure to beat the crowds, and rent a horse for the steepest stretch if needed.

attractions.name: Pisac Market
attractions.description: The Sacred Valley town of Pisac hosts a sprawling handicraft market where weavers sell alpaca textiles, ceramics and silver around a shady plaza, with clay-oven empanada bakeries tucked into the lanes. Above town, terraced Inca ruins curve along the mountainside for spectacular hiking.
attractions.bookingTip: Come on Sunday for the fullest market, and take a taxi up to the ruins first so you can hike back down into town.

attractions.name: Salt Mines of Maras
attractions.description: Thousands of shimmering salt pools cascade down a Sacred Valley hillside, fed by a single salty spring and worked by local families since before the Incas. The patchwork of white and caramel terraces is mesmerizing from the viewpoint above.
attractions.bookingTip: Pair it with the circular Inca terraces of Moray nearby on a half-day trip, and buy pink salt directly from the cooperative shop.

hotels.name: Palacio Hanan Pacha
hotels.description: A 16th-century colonial palace built on Inca foundations, where rooms receive enriched oxygen to ease the altitude and a stone-vaulted spa offers coca-leaf massages. Candlelit dinners are served in the arcaded courtyard around a colonial fountain.

hotels.name: Casa Kantu San Blas
hotels.description: A whitewashed hillside house with blue shutters, where rooms are dressed in textiles from a Chinchero weaving cooperative and terraces look over the city's rooftops. Staff tuck hot-water bottles into the beds on cold nights.

hotels.name: Tambo Mochilero
hotels.description: A friendly hostel in an old colonial house, with heated dorms, a courtyard for morning coca tea and a travel desk that books Machu Picchu logistics at fair prices. The vibe is social but calm, so you can actually sleep before a 4 a.m. trek.

hotels.name: Casona del Puma Dorado
hotels.description: A carefully restored 17th-century mansion with painted colonial murals, wooden balconies and two stone courtyards, steps from a quiet upper-town plaza. Fireplaces warm the lounge and many of the rooms on chilly nights.

hotels.name: Qolqa Riverside Retreat
hotels.description: Adobe casitas scattered through orchards on the banks of the Urubamba River, with a heated pool, hot tub and spa facing the Pisac terraces. At around 2,950 meters, it's an ideal base for acclimatizing before tackling Cusco.

hotels.name: Miradores de San Cristóbal
hotels.description: Compact apartments with kitchenettes and picture windows on the hillside below Sacsayhuamán, looking straight across the city's terracotta roofs. It's a short but steep walk down to the Plaza de Armas.

restaurants.name: Caldos Mama Sabina
restaurants.description: A steaming counter in the old market district where locals start the day with enormous bowls of hen soup, served with a boiled egg, noodles and a sliver of rocoto on the side. Sit on the bench and point at whatever your neighbor is having.

restaurants.name: Anticuchería Fogón de la Esquina
restaurants.description: Evenings on this corner mean charcoal smoke, glowing grills and skewers of marinated beef heart served with potatoes and fiery ají. Grab a cup of hot, herbal emoliente from the cart next door to warm your hands.
restaurants.signatureDish: Anticuchos de corazón (beef heart skewers) with ají

restaurants.name: Café Balcón Azul
restaurants.description: A tiny café with a blue wooden balcony over the San Blas plaza, serving Peruvian coffee from the Quillabamba valley, quinoa pancakes and fresh papaya juice. It's the perfect place to wait out an afternoon shower.
restaurants.signatureDish: Quinoa pancakes with Andean honey and coca tea

restaurants.name: Kallpa Mesa Andina
restaurants.description: An intimate tasting menu that journeys from Amazonian cacao to high-puna herbs, built around dozens of native potato and corn varieties grown by nearby communities. Each course arrives on ceramics by Andean potters, paired with Peruvian wines and creative takes on chicha.
restaurants.signatureDish: Alpaca loin with native potato purée and huacatay

restaurants.name: Rumi Balcón
restaurants.description: An upstairs dining room with a carved wooden balcony facing the cathedral, where Andean ingredients get a modern touch: quinoa risotto, crisp trout and pisco sours infused with wild mint. Book a balcony table for sunset.
restaurants.signatureDish: Quinoa-crusted Andean trout with rocoto sauce

restaurants.name: Picantería Wayta Mama
restaurants.description: A boisterous family picantería where weekend crowds share clay pots of adobo, chicharrón and oven-roasted guinea pig, washed down with frothy chicha de jora. Portions are huge and prices are strictly local.
restaurants.signatureDish: Cuy al horno with rocoto relleno

restaurants.name: Forno San Blas
restaurants.description: A cozy stone-walled pizzeria whose clay oven doubles as the room's heater on cold Andean nights. Try the pie topped with smoked alpaca and Andean cheese, or keep it classic with a margherita.
restaurants.signatureDish: Wood-fired pizza with smoked alpaca and Andean cheese

restaurants.name: Chakra & Fogón
restaurants.description: A garden restaurant beside its own organic plots, where lamb, pork and native potatoes are slow-cooked with herbs beneath hot stones in a traditional earth oven. Tables sit among the flowers with the Pisac terraces towering overhead.
restaurants.signatureDish: Pachamanca of lamb, pork, fava beans and native potatoes

experiences.name: Machu Picchu Archaeologist-Led Day Trip
experiences.description: Ride a panoramic train down the Urubamba gorge, bus up the switchbacks and explore the citadel with an archaeologist who brings the Inca world to life. Small groups and pre-booked timed entry mean more time among the terraces and less in queues.

experiences.name: Rainbow Mountain Dawn Trek
experiences.description: Leave Cusco at 4 a.m., breakfast in a highland village, then climb past grazing alpacas to the striped summit ahead of the crowds. Your guide carries emergency oxygen and sets a steady, altitude-friendly pace.

experiences.name: Backstrap Loom Weaving Workshop
experiences.description: Join a Quechua weaving family in their courtyard to wash alpaca wool with a natural root soap, dye it with cochineal and native plants, and try your hand at a backstrap loom. You'll leave with a small woven band and new respect for the prices at the market.

experiences.name: Market Bites & Pisco Tasting Walk
experiences.description: Graze through the old market district on exotic fruits like lúcuma and granadilla, giant-kernel corn, fresh cheeses and the famous round breads of nearby Oropesa. Finish in a hidden bar with a guided pisco tasting and a lesson in shaking the perfect pisco sour.
